opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the starting point is to recognize that a single model, no matter how good it is, is rarely going to give you everything you need for a real application. When you look at what people are actually deploying, it's almost always a system: you have one or more models, you have retrieval, you have tools, maybe a code interpreter, some verifiers, some guardrails. So the question becomes, how do you put these components together so that the whole thing is reliable, efficient, and something you can actually reason about?

The way I think about it, a lot of it comes back to classic systems design principles. First, modularity. You want to decompose the problem into pieces that each do something well-defined, so you can test them, swap them out, and improve them independently. If a better embedding model comes out, or a cheaper LLM that's good enough for one sub-task, you want to be able to drop it in without rebuilding everything.

Second, you have to think about the trade-offs explicitly: quality, latency, and cost. These systems open up a big design space. You can call a big model once, or a smaller model many times and vote, or route easy queries to a cheap model and hard ones to an expensive one. Each choice moves you around on that trade-off curve, and the right point depends on the application. A lot of the interesting work is in optimizing that, ideally automatically, the way a database query optimizer picks a plan for you.

Third, and this is one I care a lot about, is reliability and debuggability. Models are probabilistic; they make mistakes. So in a compound system, errors can compound too. You need ways to verify intermediate outputs, to check constraints, to fall back when something goes wrong. And you need observability, so when the final answer is bad you can figure out which component caused it. That's very hard today, and I think it's one of the big open problems.

And finally, there's the infrastructure side. These systems are heterogeneous: GPUs for some components, CPUs for others, different scaling characteristics, lots of fan-out and fan-in. That's a lot of what we were thinking about with Ray, how to give developers a simple programming model for distributed, heterogeneous workloads so they can focus on the logic of the application rather than the plumbing.

So in short: decompose, make the trade-offs explicit and optimizable, build in verification and observability from the start, and have infrastructure that makes composing all of this easy. That's how I think we get from impressive demos to systems people can actually depend on.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it, a compound AI system is just that — it's a system. It's not one model answering a question. It's a model, or several models, plus retrieval, plus tools, plus some control logic that decides what to call when, and then usually some verification or ranking at the end. And once you frame it that way, a lot of the design questions stop being machine learning questions and start being systems questions, which is what I've spent most of my career on.

So the first thing I think about is: what is the task, and where does the quality actually come from? Because people assume the quality comes from the biggest model, and often it doesn't. If you look at something like our chatbot arena work, or earlier what we saw with Vicuna, a smaller model with the right context, the right retrieval, the right prompt can beat a much bigger model on a narrow task. So you decompose the problem. Which parts need reasoning, which parts are really lookup, which parts are just formatting. And then you route accordingly. That's the whole idea behind RouteLLM, for example — you don't send every query to the most expensive model, you send the hard ones there and the easy ones somewhere cheaper, and you can cut cost by a very large factor with almost no quality loss.

The second thing is that you have to design for the fact that the components are unreliable and they're going to change. The model will be swapped out in six months. The retrieval index will drift. So you want clean interfaces between components, and you want to be able to evaluate each piece independently — and evaluate the system end to end, because they're different things. One of the lessons from Spark and from Ray is that composability only works if the abstractions are right. If you tie everything to one model's quirks, you're going to rewrite it.

Third is latency and cost as first-class constraints, not afterthoughts. In a compound system you might make five, ten, twenty model calls per user request. Some of those can run in parallel, some are sequential, some can be cached. That's a scheduling problem. That's a serving problem — it's why we care so much about things like vLLM, because the inference layer is where a lot of the cost lives, and if the system is calling the model many times, the efficiency of each call gets multiplied.

And then the last piece, which I think is underrated, is verification. If you can check the answer — run the code, run the tests, compare against a database, have another model grade it — then you can afford to generate multiple candidates and pick the best one. That's a very powerful pattern. You trade compute for reliability, and reliability is what people actually pay for in production.

So to summarize: decompose the task, route to the cheapest thing that works, keep the interfaces clean so you can swap components, treat cost and latency as design inputs, and verify wherever you can. It really is systems design. The models are components, powerful components, but the system is what delivers the value.

astra-6.text:
I think you start with the task. What are you trying to achieve, and what are the constraints? You care about the quality of the answer, but you also care about latency and cost. And then the question is: what combination of components gets you the best result within those constraints?

The language model is one component. You may also have retrieval, tools, a database, or a component that checks the result. Take a question-answering application over your company’s documents. You need to find the right documents, provide the relevant information to the model, and generate an answer. If the answer is wrong, it may be because the model made a mistake, but it may also be because you retrieved the wrong information. A better model will not necessarily fix that.

So you have to evaluate the system end to end, and then understand where the failures come from. Start with a simple design, measure it, and add complexity where it actually helps. The interesting challenge is that these choices interact. You can spend more on retrieval and use a smaller model, or call a model multiple times to improve an answer. You are optimizing a system, and the model is one of the things you can change.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the starting point is that you are designing a system, not just choosing a model. You have an application, you have a quality target, and you have constraints on latency and cost. Then you ask: what combination of components can meet those requirements? That might include a language model, retrieval, tools, and some way to check the result.

The interesting part is that these choices interact. A better retriever might let you use a smaller model. An additional verification step might improve quality, but it also adds latency and cost. So you need to evaluate the entire system on the task you care about, identify where it fails, and optimize from there.

And I would start simple. Add complexity when you can measure the benefit. Otherwise, you can build a very complicated system without knowing which parts are actually helping.
